summary:
Krasnodar Krai stands under the national framework of Russia, where same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. Public expression 'promoting' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the 'gay propaganda' law by fines or detention of up to 15 days, and a repeated offence risks criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. A visitor whose documents or appearance do not match carries exposure under a statute that has no exemption for foreigners.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel. It warns all travellers, regardless of personal characteristic, of wrongful detention and arbitrary law enforcement, and states that foreigners found guilty under the propaganda law face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation; the advisory carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Federal extremism enforcement applies nationwide, Krasnodar Krai included. As of 30 June 2025 Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated 'international LGBT movement' or for displaying its alleged symbols, and 81 people convicted of administrative offences in 98 court cases since January 2024 for displaying those symbols, mostly on social media. The 2023 Supreme Court designation of the movement as extremist enabled criminal prosecutions carrying up to 12 years in prison, building on the 2013 'gay propaganda' law.

Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws, including convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions, according to the UK government country policy and information note of June 2025.

Enforcement is expanding in volume as well as severity. Cases under the propaganda laws grew eighteenfold over the past decade, Meduza reported on 19 June 2025, and fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.
tangentialFactors:
The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as 'a second-class citizen' after the extremist designation.

In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed 'Ada', a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v2.0, June 2025, page updated 12 August 2026) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.
localsOnly:
Residents of Krasnodar Krai have no statutory protection on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity: the Russian constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people, and same-sex marriage has no legal standing.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year, removing both a route to amend official documents and access to medical transition within the domestic system.

Liability under the propaganda statutes attaches to residents as well as visitors: fines or detention of up to 15 days for a first public expression, and criminal prosecution with up to four years' imprisonment for a repeated offence.

Since the 2023 Supreme Court designation of the 'international LGBT movement' as extremist, residents face criminal charges carrying up to 12 years in prison for participation in the group or display of its alleged symbols. Human Rights Watch counted 101 such convictions as of 30 June 2025, alongside 81 people convicted of administrative offences in 98 court cases since January 2024 for displaying those symbols, most often on social media.

Enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws affected at least 139 people across Russia between 2022 and 2024 through convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions, and propaganda-law cases have grown eighteenfold over the past decade.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no Krasnodar-Krai-specific enforcement figures, raid records or reporting on local police practice; every case count cited here is federal in scope, and the Moscow, St Petersburg and Novosibirsk incidents took place in other regions.

Whether regional statutes or policing directives in Krasnodar Krai impose obligations beyond the federal framework is not sourced. No information was found on local hate-crime sentencing outcomes or on documented violence against trans people in the Krai.

The inventory does not describe how Russian border or document checks treat foreign-issued identity papers whose gender marker differs from the holder's presentation. Screening at the point of entry, and any risk of being outed during it, remain unresolved questions here.

Two open questions remain unresolved as to practice rather than law: the availability and cost of legal representation for a foreigner detained under the propaganda statutes in this Krai, and whether consular notification is reliably triggered in such detentions.
